notes: Only possible staggered angle is Table 6 (lobbyist switches between external and in-house; 7% of lobbyists switch, 56% always in-house, i.e., always-treated); it includes Tenure_it, so it would fail the controls rule anyway.
data_statement: No data or code availability statement; data are public SOPR lobbying disclosure reports, GPO congressional hearing transcripts, and RegData 2.2, hand-matched to firms via ORBIS/COMPUSTAT/web sources.

design: Telecom subscribers offered a free 60 MB mobile-data trial in a single promotion month (month 2); offer takers (self-selected) versus nontakers compared between month 1 and month 3.
reason: There is one promotion date for everyone and only one pre and one post period, so treatment timing is not staggered. Estimation is Athey-Imbens changes-in-changes (mean and quantile; Tables 5-12) plus a two-period DID column, and Table 3 is a probit of take-up; offer assignment was randomized.
appendix_only_specs: none (Appendices A-B report first-step regressions for conditional CIC).
notes: Redemption dates vary only within days 7-13 of month 2, but the analysis uses a single pre/post month pair.
data_statement: Proprietary call-record data from an unnamed telecom operator under nondisclosure restrictions; no data availability statement; authors used MATLAB CIC code from Susan Athey's website (https://athey.people.stanford.edu/research).

design: Loan-level data on 43,771 agricultural crop loans by 44 loan officers in 14 Indian bank branches (2005-2012); treatment indicators flag loans originated in the last N months of an officer's expected 36-month tenure (or loans that straddle the officer's rotation), so the indicator switches on at officer-specific calendar dates; comparison is loans made earlier in tenure and loans by other officers.
reason: If the tenure-based indicator is read as a staggered binary adoption (officer-specific switch-on dates under mandatory rotation), every main-text specification violates the rules: Tables 3, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9 all include time-varying loan controls (Loan Size, Current Tenure, Repeated), several add officer-by-month FE, and the 'calendar month' FE appear to be month-of-year rather than calendar-time FE (they coexist with year FE and officer-by-month FE that would otherwise absorb the treatment); Table 4 is a local window around actual rotation dates with officer and year FE plus controls; Table 10 is cross-sectional. If the lead does not treat a tenure-position indicator as an adoption design, the paper is ineligible.
appendix_only_specs: Online appendix Table A.19 reportedly re-estimates the main results without Loan Size and Current Tenure (numbers not in main text); other appendix tables cluster at officer level, split busy/lean seasons and branches, and use days outstanding.
notes: Units are loans (repeated cross-sections assigned to officers); Straddle is defined ex post from actual rotation dates; all officers in the scheduled-rotation sample are eventually treated. Figure 2 plots 15 separate before/after regressions by tenure month k.
data_statement: Proprietary loan-account data provided by an Indian public-sector bank via the Center for Analytical Finance, Indian School of Business; no data or code availability statement.

design: Garment-factory study with (i) worker-date personnel data where supervisor gender varies as supervisors rotate through one line and (ii) a lab-in-the-field experiment randomly assigning workers to male or female supervisors and randomly restricting supervisor scut work.
reason: The causal evidence is a randomized experiment (Tables 4-5, OLS with phase FE on 189 worker-session observations). The personnel-data analysis (Figure 1, Appendix B) is a seasonal-adjusted mean comparison where supervisor gender switches back and forth with rotation, not a staggered adoption design.
appendix_only_specs: Appendix B plots within-worker mean productivity by supervisor gender (no regression table); Appendix E is an experimental regression.
notes: none
data_statement: Supplemental material states 'The data file is available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2020.3639'; data are proprietary factory personnel records plus the authors' experiment.

design: Loan-month hazard panel of 194,026 Pennsylvania mortgages originated 2004-2006 and followed through 2012; treatment Any Fracking switches on in the month a ZIP code receives its first fracking permit (ZIP-specific dates, mostly 2008-2012); comparison is never-fracked and not-yet-fracked ZIP codes.
reason: The binary staggered design is present (Table 4 cols 5-6 use county or ZIP FE plus year-month FE), but every main-text specification includes a quadratic in mortgage age (time-varying) and columns 2-8 add loan-level underwriting covariates; column 1 has duration only and no unit or time FE; columns 7-8 and Tables 7-10 are IV (shale geology x permits); Table 6 adds the time-varying Underwater indicator and its interaction. The outcome is a first-delinquency hazard, so loans exit after the event.
appendix_only_specs: Internet appendix has alternative fracking measures (IV), subsample restrictions, a 2001-recession placebo, prepayment and competing-risk (multinomial logit) models, and a Cox model; none described as a plain TWFE without covariates.
notes: Closest spec: Table 4 col 6 (ZIP FE + year-month FE, Any Fracking -0.093 (0.024), in basis points) but it carries mortgage-age polynomial and underwriting controls.
data_statement: No availability statement; uses proprietary McDash Analytics mortgage data and Equifax CRISM, plus public PA DEP permit data, IRS SOI, BLS, and EIA shale maps; article is in the public domain (U.S. government employees).

design: User-day panel of about 29.7 million NYT readers (April-October 2013); the June 2013 mobile-app paywall change reaches each user when they update the app (days 95-120), so PaywallPolicy_it switches on at user-specific dates; subscribers (unaffected) serve as the comparison group.
reason: Staggered binary exposure via app-update timing exists, but every main-text specification violates a rule: readership models (Tables 2-5, 8, 9, 12) are Poisson; all specifications include both PaywallPolicy_it and its interaction with NotSubscribed_i (or with post-treatment behavioral subgroups or continuous prior readership), i.e., subgroup-by-treatment interactions and continuous intensity (Tables 6, 7, 13); Table 11 is logit. The only linear readership model (Table 10, log(1+articles) with user and day FE) still has the PaywallPolicy main effect plus the NotSubscribed interaction.
appendix_only_specs: Appendix Tables A.1-A.6 report intent-to-treat versions assuming a common update date (single date), same specifications.
notes: Closest spec: Table 10 col 1, ln(NumArticlesTotal+1), PaywallPolicy 0.006 (1.1E-04), PaywallPolicy x NotSubscribed -0.072 (3.2E-04), user and day FE. Readership sample drops users who changed subscription status.
data_statement: Proprietary NYT user-level activity data (first author was NYT scholar-in-residence in 2013); no data or code availability statement.

design: Employee-month panel (2006-2010) of 2,466 idea-submitting employees at a European car-parts manufacturer; Post-assignment switches on after an employee's first interplant assignment (employee-specific months); never-assigned employees (and CEM-matched controls) are the comparison.
reason: The staggered binary design is present with employee FE and year-month FE, but every main-text specification (Tables 4, 5, 6) adds time-varying controls built from past outcomes (Ideas submitted, Last idea submission, Previous ideas submitted, Previous implementation rate, Previous average idea value, Repeated assignments) and a contemporaneous on/off Assignment dummy (additional treatment). The DD columns are matching-based (CEM) with treatment-by-matched-status interactions, and Table 6 splits treatment into four direction-specific dummies.
appendix_only_specs: Online appendix has robustness checks and Monte Carlo sensitivity to unobserved assignments; nothing described as a plain TWFE without controls.
notes: Closest spec: Table 4 FE column, Post-assignment 23.72 (6.97) with Assignment 151.34 (56.30) and controls. Repeat assignments occur (336 assignments by 222 employees).
data_statement: Proprietary idea-database data from an unnamed firm; no data or code availability statement (article is open access under CC BY-NC-ND).

design: Patient-visit cross-section of 377,346 adult ED attendances (2007-2013) at one UK hospital whose clinical decision unit operated throughout; treatment is a patient's routing to the CDU.
reason: No policy adoption or staggered timing: the CDU existed for the whole period and treatment is patient-level routing. Estimation is probit, recursive bivariate probit with instruments (Tables 5, 7), and Heckman probit (Table 8), followed by counterfactual simulations (Table 6).
appendix_only_specs: E-companion has nearest-neighbor matching and alternative outcome definitions; not DiD.
notes: none
data_statement: Proprietary hospital ED and inpatient records from a UK NHS trust; no data or code availability statement.

design: 7,411 malpractice claims (repeated cross-sections) against 161 Florida hospitals, injuries 1999-2007; treatment is hospital use of basic or advanced EMRs at the time of injury, adopted in hospital-specific years (12 none-to-basic, 53 none-to-advanced, 50 basic-to-advanced, 7 never, 13 always advanced); comparison is not-yet and never adopters.
reason: Staggered adoption with hospital FE and year FE is the stated DiD design (Table 6), but every main-text specification includes time-varying hospital covariates (Employees, Working Hours per Patient, Salary per FTE, Net Revenue per Patient, Occupancy, Geographic Index, Case Mix Index) and claim covariates (Claim Load, Monetary Size, Claim Defendants, severity dummies), and enters two treatment indicators (Basic EMR and Advanced EMR). The Model 3 event study (basic-EMR leads/lags) keeps the same controls; Table 8 adds hazard, negative binomial, and hospital-specific trends; Tables 9-11 are control-laden subsamples.
appendix_only_specs: none reported; text mentions an unreported trend model without hospital covariates ('similar results', no numbers).
notes: Closest spec: Table 6 Model 1, Basic EMR -141.123 (38.864), Advanced EMR -250.928 (40.921). Many hospitals already had basic EMRs at the start (always-treated for the basic indicator). Outcome indexed by injury year; year indicators reflect filing year.
data_statement: No availability statement; claims are public records from the Florida Office of Insurance Regulation (https://apps.fldfs.com/PLCR/Search/MPLClaim.aspx), EMR adoption from the proprietary HIMSS Analytics database, hospital characteristics from Florida AHCA reports.

design: Continuous-time industry equilibrium model of markups with calibration; empirical part is an industry-year panel (1998-2017) relating repurchases and cash holdings to continuous product-fluidity measures and their interaction with a 2008-2009 crisis dummy.
reason: Primarily a theory and calibration paper (Sections 2-4.2, Tables 1 and 3, Figures 1-5). The empirical Tables 2 and 4 use continuous fluidity regressors, a single common crisis window, time FE only, and many time-varying industry controls; there is no binary staggered treatment.
appendix_only_specs: Online Appendix A.2 reports firm-level versions of the fluidity regressions; not DiD.
notes: none
data_statement: No data or code availability statement; uses Compustat and the Hoberg-Phillips-Prabhala product-fluidity measure (no URL given).

design: Two-wave randomized field experiment (2013 and 2014 tax years) assigning Ontario organizations that filed the employer health tax late to a standard or a planning-prompt late notice (40/60 split), randomized independently each year.
reason: Treatment is randomly assigned letter type within each wave with a common mailing date; analyses are t-tests, chi-square tests, multinomial logit, and OLS with letter-by-prior-exposure interactions (Table 1, Appendix Table A3). No staggered adoption design.
appendix_only_specs: none
notes: none
data_statement: Administrative tax data from the Government of Ontario (Ministry of Finance partnership); no data or code availability statement (article is open access under CC BY-NC-ND).

design: Event-window study of CDS spread changes for 500 U.S. firms around 12,716 dividend announcements (2001-2014); the 'treatment' is a per-announcement cut/raise dummy (repeated, non-absorbing events), with no adoption date or untreated comparison panel.
reason: There is no staggered binary adoption: each observation is one announcement window and CutD/RaiseD classify the announcement. Tables 2, 4, 7-9 are univariate window means, and the regressions in Tables 3-7 include year and firm FE plus time-varying controls (EarnSur, dEarnings, dVolatility) and subgroup interactions (Recession, credit risk, NegPastRet).
appendix_only_specs: Online appendix Table IA.8 runs a propensity-score-matched treated/control CutD x Post regression on spreads at day -8 and +7 (matching-based, single event window per firm); not eligible either.
notes: Announcement-level event study; not a panel DiD design.
data_statement: No data or code availability statement; data come from Markit (CDS), CRSP, Compustat, the WRDS Intraday Indicator database, and covenant-violation data from Amir Sufi's website.

design: County-quarter panel of 3,107 U.S. counties (2005Q2-2014Q4); treated counties received a complete 2006 TIGER map when the whole U.S. was seeded into OpenStreetMap at one date (late 2007/2008Q1), controls received the outdated map at the same date.
reason: Treatment timing is common to all treated counties (single Post = after 2007Q4), so this is a 2x2 DiD with county and quarter FE (Table 3, Table 5 panel A, Table 7), not staggered adoption. Table 4 and Table 6 are cross-sectional regressions and Figure 4 is a single-date event study.
appendix_only_specs: Online appendix Tables D.2-D.7 (IV with treatment dummy, Google Trends controls, object-level Florida cross-section); none staggered.
notes: Would otherwise be a clean TWFE (Table 3 col 1: Post x Treat on log total contributions, -0.471 (0.0466), county and quarter FE, no controls), but adoption is not staggered. The paper links a public replication archive on OSF despite having no INFORMS package.
data_statement: Public repository stated: 'Code and data to replicate the analysis in the paper can be found at https://osf.io/a47e9/.' Schedule data on MTAIP county updates are described as proprietary data obtained from Census Bureau officials.

design: Model-city-month vehicle sales in four Chinese cities (Mar 2012-Feb 2013) before and after the nationwide anti-Japan boycott starting September 2012; every brand is exposed at the same date and the authors state they have no control group.
reason: Single common event date with an explicit before-and-after design (Section 5: 'we do not have a control group... a difference-in-differences method is not feasible'). Tables 4-8 estimate Berry-logit demand regressions of Boycott (or news count) x country-of-origin with model-year and city-quarter FE plus advertising regressors (instrumented in places).
appendix_only_specs: none
notes: Treatment is also continuous in several columns (log monthly news count).
data_statement: No data or code availability statement; sales from R.L. Polk & Company, advertising from CTR Market Research, quality from J.D. Power IQS, news counts from the China Digital Library (proprietary sources).

design: Firm-year panel of Colombian firms in war zones (2010-2016); treated = firms in FARC-dominated areas, controls = firms in ELN-dominated areas, single treatment date = the November 2012 FARC peace-process announcement.
reason: All treated firms switch on at the same date, so the main DiD (Tables 7-12, 15-17: FARC x AFTER with time FE and municipality/firm controls such as assets, leverage, ROI) is a single-date design, not staggered. The attack-level extension (Tables 13-14) uses propensity-score and nearest-neighbor matching on firm-years exposed to a nearby attack in the prior year, which is matching-based and non-absorbing.
appendix_only_specs: Online appendix parallel-trend tests, placebo and alternative specifications; all around the single 2012 date.
notes: Main specs also include time-varying controls and no firm FE (FARC level dummy plus time FE).
data_statement: No public repository; firm data come from the Colombia Ministry of Trade business census, kept confidential and accessed via a scientific data-access request, plus Memoria Historica attack data and the University of Los Andes municipal panel.

design: U.S. manufacturing plant-year panel (ASM/CMF/LBD, 1976-2004); treatment = plant's four-digit SIC industry experienced a large import-tariff cut in t, t-1, or t-2, with cuts occurring in different industries in different years (Figure 1); comparison = plants in industries without a recent cut, with conglomerate vs. stand-alone plants as the key contrast.
reason: The design is staggered and binary at the industry level, but every main-text specification adds time-varying controls: lagged plant size and plant age plus the industry-state-year mean of the dependent variable (Tables 3, 4, 10, 11), size/age controls with firm FE (Tables 5, 6, 8), or time-varying industry size and share variables (Table 9). Most specifications also add a Treated x Conglomerate (or Core/Noncore, TFP tercile) subgroup interaction; even the Table 3 subsample columns (2)-(3), which have plant FE, state x year FE and Treated alone, keep the size/age controls.
appendix_only_specs: none tabulated in an appendix; footnote 30 says results are unchanged when the industry-state-year means are dropped, but size and age controls remain.
notes: Treatment indicator is a three-year window that switches off after t+2 and industries may experience repeated cuts; regressions are weighted by ASM sampling weights. Table 7 is a matched-sample decomposition. Table 1 is a logit/probit/LPM predictability check.
data_statement: No data or code availability statement; plant data are confidential U.S. Census microdata (ASM, CMF, LBD) accessed in a Federal Statistical Research Data Center, and tariff data are public from the NBER and UC Davis Center for International Data.

design: Analytical two-period Salop model of advertising, pricing, and user-generated ratings/reviews; no empirical panel or treatment.
reason: Pure theory paper (Propositions 1-7, Sections 3-4); there are no regressions in the main text.
appendix_only_specs: Online appendix contains a small descriptive comparison of rating trends for 10 products on Amazon vs. Walmart.com (Section 5.1 mentions it); not a DiD.
notes: Theory.
data_statement: None stated; no data used in the main text.

design: Analytical Hotelling model of two competing media platforms choosing traditional vs. sponsored-content advertising; no empirical data.
reason: Pure theory paper (Propositions 1-5); the phrase 'difference-in-difference comparison' in Section 5.1 refers to comparing model welfare thresholds, not an estimation.
appendix_only_specs: none
notes: Theory.
data_statement: None stated; no data used.

design: Firm-quarter panel of U.S. repurchasing firms (1984-2016) relating the probability of future repurchases to the continuous gain/loss on past repurchased stock (REPO_RET) and a LOSS dummy; no adoption event.
reason: Treatment is continuous (REPO_RET) interacted with a time-varying LOSS indicator that switches on and off, estimated with conditional firm or CEO fixed-effects logit (Tables 3-6) with many time-varying controls; Table 7 compares timing returns, Table 8 compensation/turnover regressions, Table 9 Fama-MacBeth regressions.
appendix_only_specs: Online appendix Tables IA.2-IA.4 (dot-com and financial-crisis subperiods, SEC monthly repurchase data); same continuous-treatment logit design.
notes: The 'difference-in-difference estimate' in Table 7 is a difference of portfolio returns, not a DiD regression.
data_statement: No data or code availability statement; data from Compustat, CRSP, Execucomp, Thomson Reuters, IRRC, compensation data from Lalitha Naveen's website, and Peters-Wagner turnover data on WRDS.

design: Block-year panel of 9,493 Landsat blocks (~100x100 miles) covering Earth's land mass, 1950-1990; treatment switches on when a block is first mapped (or first mapped with a low-cloud image) by Landsats 1-3, with first-mapping years spread from 1972 through 1983; blocks never mapped in the first phase stay untreated throughout, and not-yet-mapped blocks serve as comparisons.
reason: Absorbing binary treatment with staggered block-specific dates. Table 2 columns 3 and 4 regress the gold-discovery indicator on Post Mapped or Post Low-Cloud with only block and year FE (OLS, SE clustered by block), and Table 3 repeats the same specification for junior- and senior-firm discoveries. Table 2 columns 1-2 (no block FE), column 5 (both treatments jointly) and Table 4 (Post x cost-group interactions) do not qualify.

design: Compustat firm-year panel 1989-1994; treated = near-insolvent firms incorporated in Delaware, controls = near-insolvent non-Delaware firms, single treatment date = the December 1991 Credit Lyonnais Delaware court ruling.
reason: One common adoption date for all treated firms, so not staggered. Main specifications (Tables 5-13, 15) are DE x POST x HIGHDP triple differences with firm and year FE plus time-varying controls (size, leverage, loss, volatility, returns, etc.); Table 8 is a single-date dynamic version and Table 17 is a probit.
appendix_only_specs: none
notes: Single-date triple difference.
data_statement: No data or code availability statement; data from Compustat and CRSP with going-concern opinions hand-collected from LexisNexis SEC filings, media counts from Factiva, and board data from Compact Disclosure.

design: Randomized controlled trial in 238 stores of an Eastern European retail chain; stores randomly assigned on September 1, 2015 to Manage, Career, Manage+Career, or control letters, with a randomized reminder to a subset in September 2016; outcome is monthly cashier quit rate.
reason: Randomized experiment with a single treatment date estimated by ANCOVA (outcome on treatment dummies, pre-period mean, time and strata FE) in Tables 3-5; Table 6 is a two-period survey DiD and Table 7 ordered logits. There is no staggered adoption.
appendix_only_specs: Online appendix II reports alternative treatment-effect estimators for the same RCT.
notes: RCT registered as AEARCTR-0000826.
data_statement: No data or code availability statement; data are the firm's proprietary personnel, accounting, and survey records, and the trial is registered in the AEA RCT Registry (AEARCTR-0000826).

design: Firm-year panel of 429 U.S. firms first targeted by activist hedge funds in 1998-2012 (event years vary by firm, Table 1) and 429 nearest-neighbor matched never-targeted control firms, observed t-3 to t+3 around each matched pair's event year.
reason: Activism dates are staggered across 1998-2012 and Table 3 estimates DHFA x POST with firm and year FE, but every column adds time-varying controls (log MVE, log age, Tobin's Q) and a pair-specific POST indicator defined in event time relative to the matched event year, i.e., a matching-based/stacked design. Tables 4, 8, 10-12 use industry rather than firm FE plus deal and firm controls; Table 5 col. 1 (LPM with firm FE) also has controls and cols. 2-3 are logit; Tables 6, 7, 9 repeat model (1) with controls and subgroup splits.
appendix_only_specs: Online appendix Tables IA.3, IA.4, IA.6-IA.10 repeat model (1) with yearly values, binary outcomes (LPM/logit), confrontational and 13G-to-13D switch samples; all described with the same controls and matched design.
notes: Control group is built by propensity/nearest-neighbor matching (Abadie-Imbens) on covariates; the panel aggregates controls to pre/post-period averages (sample size 1,575). Also a 13G-to-13D switch test with hedge fund FE (model 8) in the appendix.
data_statement: None stated; data come from SharkRepellent, CRSP/Compustat, Thomson Reuters SDC and ownership, I/B/E/S (proprietary), an activist hedge fund list shared by Alon Brav, and forced CEO turnover data shared by Florian Peters.

design: About 14,000 U.S. manufacturing establishments observed only in 2005 and 2010 (MOPS recall question); treated = acquired between 2006 and 2010, control = not acquired; estimated as a two-period change regression.
reason: With only two observed periods, every acquired establishment is untreated in 2005 and treated in 2010, so there is a single effective adoption cohort; Table 6 (eq. 2) is a 2x2 DiD in first differences with industry and state FE and time-varying controls in changes (cols. 2-5). Table 6 col. 5 splits acquisitions into 2006-08 vs 2009-10, but no intermediate periods are observed. Tables 4, 5, 9 are cross-sectional LPMs, Table 8 is an acquired-only two-period panel, Table 10 compares completed vs withdrawn deals, Tables 12-13 use a continuous interaction.
appendix_only_specs: Online appendix Tables A3-A6 (per-question outcomes, timing split for performance, recall-bias controls) use the same two-period change design.
notes: Table 6 col. 1 (state FE only, no controls) is a clean two-period DiD, coefficient 0.0254 (0.0048), but not staggered.
data_statement: Confidential U.S. Census Bureau microdata (MOPS, ASM, LBD) used under disclosure review; no public data or code availability stated.

design: Firm-year panel of 200 media-identified 'Olympic stocks' in five host countries whose winning bids were announced on different dates (Sydney 1993, Athens 1997, Beijing 2001, London 2005, Rio 2009), compared with 200 propensity-score-matched non-Olympic stocks in the same country and industry, from three years before each bid to three years after the games.
reason: Treatment (Olympic stock x post-bid period) switches on at five distinct country-specific dates with never-treated matched controls, so the design is staggered and binary. But every main-text regression (Tables 2, 3, 4, 6, 7, 9) uses country, year and industry FE instead of firm FE, includes time-varying firm controls (log assets, log market cap, B/M, E/P, ROA, CFO, sales growth), and defines periods in event time relative to each Olympics (middle/Olympic/postgame), i.e., a matched stacked design; Table 5 is cross-sectional and Table 8 covers single Olympics.
appendix_only_specs: Online appendix referenced only generically; CEM-matching robustness and Tokyo/stay-at-home extensions are untabulated or figures only (Figures 6-7).
notes: Treatment also switches off after the games (separate Olympic x postgame-years interaction). Main outcome is a constructed firm-year comovement R2 relative to Olympic vs non-Olympic indices. Could alternatively be read as ineligible because each Olympics is analyzed as its own matched event window; I classify near-miss because the five cohorts are staggered and binary.
data_statement: Open-access article (CC BY 4.0) with no data or code availability statement; stock and accounting data from FactSet, media counts from Factiva (proprietary), plus hand-collected Olympic stock lists.

design: Cross-section of 3,656 major-regional airline outsourced routes in fall 2006; outcome is whether the route is still outsourced to the same regional in fall 2010; key regressors are continuous network-weather proxies for relationship value.
reason: There is no DiD: Tables 4 and 5 regress a 2006-2010 survival dummy on continuous network weather measures with major, regional, route, and major-route FE. The authors state that because the 2008 crisis did not differentially affect groups of routes 'we cannot use a traditional difference-in-differences estimation approach' (Section 6.2); the shock is a single common date and the regressor is continuous.
appendix_only_specs: Online appendix Tables A6-A9 (probit, subsamples, hub weather, multinomial logit) are cross-sectional as well.
notes: The article's supplemental-material line says data files are posted at the journal DOI, which conflicts with the batch's 'no package' status; the lead may want to check the INFORMS page.
data_statement: The article states 'The data files and online appendix are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2021.3970'; underlying data are BTS DB1B and T100, Regional Airline Association, NOAA weather, and FAA ground-delay data obtained through a FOIA request.

design: Monthly customer panel (September 2013 to June 2015) of about 280,000 'poked' customers on 13 legacy price plans, all notified by SMS in March 2014 of a May 2014 price change, versus about 632,000 non-poked customers of the same European mobile operator.
reason: All treated customers are notified in the same month (March 2014), so there is a single adoption date; the event-study DiD in eq. (1) (Figures 2-6, A.3-A.5) uses time FE, a poked dummy, and age, gender, and postal-code income controls. No staggered timing anywhere in the paper.
appendix_only_specs: Online appendix results with exact churn dates and all customers repeat the same single-date design.
notes: No unit FE; group dummy only.
data_statement: Proprietary customer-level data from an unnamed European mobile operator under a nondisclosure agreement, plus a Kantar survey; no data availability statement.

design: Daily time series of sovereign and financial-sector CDS spreads for 17 countries, January 2006 to December 2017, modeled with a quantile factor VAR.
reason: Methods paper that develops quantile connectedness for VARs with common factors; there is no treatment, no panel DiD, and results are spillover indices and network statistics (Figures 4-13, Tables 2-3).
appendix_only_specs: none
data_statement: No data availability statement; CDS data from Markit (proprietary) and synthetic financial-sector indices from Greenwood-Nimmo et al. (2019); the article says 'Computer code written for R is available on request.'

design: Disease-category-by-hospital-year panel (192 hospitals in FL, AZ, MD, KY, 2004-2013) where hospitals adopt CPOE systems in different years (staggered binary, abandoners dropped), compared with not-yet and never adopters; a state-level Recovery Audit Program also starts in 2005 (FL), 2007 (AZ), 2010 (MD, KY).
reason: CPOE adoption is staggered and binary with hospital-disease-category and year FE (eq. 1), but every main-text specification also includes 'Other EHR systems' (time-varying share of four other EHR systems, an additional treatment), and all except Table 3 col. 1 add time-varying hospital controls (discharges, bed days) and county characteristics x year; most columns add Audit and CPOE x Audit. Table 7's relative-time model includes controls and audit interactions, Table 5 adds neighbors' CPOE, Table 8 is CEM-matched, Table 10 is IV.
appendix_only_specs: Online appendix Tables A1-A2 (all EHR systems), D (post-2007 subsample), E (excluding Maryland), C (CEM balance); all with the same controls.

design: Physician-year (Table 2) and county-year (Table 3) panels, 2015-2019, restricted to counties on DMA borders; the regressor is continuous annual per-capita drug-injury TV ad spending in the DMA, with physician (or county) FE and border-by-year FE; there is no binary adoption event.
reason: Treatment is a continuous intensity (ad dollars per capita), not a binary switch-on at adoption dates. Table 2 (cols 1-4) regresses NOAC, warfarin, total, and placebo fills on DI ads per capita with physician and border-year FE. Table 3 (cols 1-6) does the same for inpatient visits and adds a DI ads x Share65+ interaction in cols 2, 4, 6. No staggered binary design exists anywhere in the paper.
appendix_only_specs: Online Appendix B.2 runs a simple TWFE with the same continuous ad regressor on the full sample and the border sample; B.6 adds lagged ads; C.1 is an IV of hospitalizations on NOAC prescriptions instrumented by ads x Share65. All use continuous treatment.
notes: This is a Shapiro (2018)-style DMA-border design with continuous advertising exposure. Table 2 col 1 NOAC coef -10.153 (SE 4.451) is shown only to document the estimand.
data_statement: The article states 'The online appendices and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2023.04294'; prescriptions and hospitalizations come from public CMS Medicare files, and the ad data are proprietary X Ante/Vivvix CMAG data that X Ante 'generously provided'.

design: Commuting-zone-by-month panel (633 CZs, 1990-2016) in which construction employment changes are regressed on continuous log rainfall predicted 1-6 months ahead from CZ-specific ENSO responses (IV), followed by a calibrated multisector labor-market model.
reason: Treatment is continuous forecasted rainfall, instrumented by ENSO x CZ indicators (Equations 1-2, Table 2 cols 1-6), with CZ-by-month-of-year FE, month FE, lagged rainfall, lagged temperature, and lagged-ENSO controls. appendix_only_specs: Table A1 regresses the quarterly wage bill on contemporaneous ENSO-driven rainfall (IV, continuous); Tables A7-A8 are model sensitivity checks. None is a DiD.
notes: The authors call the first stage 'a type of difference-in-differences estimator', but it is an IV with continuous, CZ-specific ENSO exposure.

design: Three independent cross-sectional conjoint surveys of Prolific respondents (353, 301, 391 usable) fielded before the Dobbs leak (Mar 26 2022), after the leak (May 7), and after the decision (Jul 9), analyzed with hierarchical-Bayes logit partworths, importance weights, and simulated vote shares.
reason: This is a single national event with repeated cross-sections of different respondents and no unit panel. Tables 3-7 report wave-to-wave differences and group differences (party, gender) in importance weights and simulated vote shares from a Bayesian logit, not linear regressions with unit and time FE. The state abortion-ban split (Table A.2) is a cross-sectional grouping, not staggered adoption.
appendix_only_specs: Table A.2 splits importance weights by state abortion-ban status (cross-sectional grouping, single event); Tables A.1 and A.3 are validity checks and share differences.
notes: The paper is about a conjoint event study around a single national event; it has no regression-based DiD.
data_statement: The article states 'The data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2023.4802' and that 'The data, code, and analyses appear at the following website: https://tinyurl.com/roe-wade-conjoint.'

design: Firm-pair-by-quarter panel (1996-2017) in which 377 firms entering or exiting the S&P 500 at different dates (firm i) are paired with every S&P 500 firm (Treat=1) and with 1,000 random firms (Treat=0); Inclusion=1 while firm i is in the index, and the estimated effect is the coefficient on Treat x Inclusion.
reason: S&P 500 entries occur at firm-specific dates, so the setting is staggered and binary. The only pooled DiD regression in the main text (Table 6) is a pair-level triple difference. Treat x Inclusion is estimated with firm-i-by-quarter and firm-j-by-quarter FE and no pair (unit) FE, the Inclusion main effect is absorbed, and identification comes from S&P peers versus random peers of the same firm-quarter: a subgroup-by-treatment interaction with nonredundant group-by-time FE. Entries and exits are pooled, so treatment also switches off. Column 2 adds time-varying pair controls (Same Analyst, Similar SIZE, etc.). The main-outcome DiDs (Tables 7-8) are one regression per event (single date each), followed by a cross-sectional regression of the 377 estimated effects. All other tables (2-5, 9) use continuous disclosure similarity.
appendix_only_specs: none
notes: Table 6 col 1 (outcome Disclosure Similarity, Treat x Inclusion, Firm i x Yearqtr FE and Firm j x Yearqtr FE, no controls) prints coef 0.019 with t = 4.28; no SE is printed, standard errors are clustered by firm i (377) and year-quarter (85), and N = 6,503,038. A lenient reading could treat firm-i-by-quarter FE as an allowed 'time-invariant characteristic x calendar time' FE. The binding problems are the triple-difference structure with no pair FE and the pooled exits that switch off. The outcome in Table 6 is the mediator (disclosure similarity), not return comovement.
data_statement: The article states 'The data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2023.4915'; the underlying data combine public EDGAR 10-K/10-Q text with Compustat, CRSP, Thomson Reuters 13F, and I/B/E/S (subscription databases).

design: Firm-by-HS4-product-category long differences (484 Taiwanese electronics firms, 181 categories, 2000 vs 2003-2011) around a single November 2001 Taiwanese policy change that lifted offshoring bans on 19 product categories; continuous log change in China offshoring is instrumented by an affected-category dummy.
reason: There is one policy date for all affected categories, and the treatment of interest is continuous offshoring estimated by IV-Poisson GMM (Tables 3, 5-8) or PPML (Tables 2, 4). Table 4 compares Taiwanese with Japanese/Korean firms in PPML long differences around the same single date. Table 5 col 9 is a panel 2SLS with firm and year FE and continuous offshoring (IV). No staggered binary adoption exists.
appendix_only_specs: Online Table A7.2 re-estimates the IV with alternative control categories (still single-date IV); Online Appendix A6 has Japanese/Korean trend figures.
notes: The authors note that export data start in 2000, which leaves one pre-period year.
data_statement: The article states 'The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.04944' (open access, CC BY 4.0); the inputs are Chinese customs data, USPTO PatentsView, PATSTAT, and the Ganglmair et al. process/product classification at https://bganglmair.github.io/data.html.

design: Fund-firm-quarter panel of ESG mutual funds' holdings in which treated firms are Russell 1000 firms whose Refinitiv ESG score rose mechanically when Refinitiv expanded coverage to Russell 3000 in 2015, and controls are firms newly added in 2015 that had prior KLD ratings; the main analysis uses a single date (Post = 2016 quarters vs 2015 quarters).
reason: The main analyses (Tables 3-7, 9; Figure 7 event study) use one adoption date for all treated firms and include the time-varying KLD Rating control, so they are not staggered. The only use of the 2015/2016/2017 expansion waves is Table 8, a stacked-cohort DiD with firm-by-cohort and fund-by-quarter-by-cohort FE plus the KLD control. That design is staggered in waves but violates the stacked and time-varying-control rules.
appendix_only_specs: Online Appendix Tables A.2-A.3 address Refinitiv data vintages, and Table A.4 is a 2018-2022 association regression (not DiD).
notes: This could reasonably be classed as ineligible. The core design is single-date, and in later waves the 'treated' firms are already-covered firms whose percentile ranks shift again, so treatment is not a clean absorbing adoption. Table 3 col 1: Perc. Holdings, Treatment x Post 0.003 (t = 2.602), Fund-YrQtr FE and Firm FE, KLD control; only t-statistics are printed.
data_statement: The article states 'The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.06184'; the inputs are CRSP Mutual Fund Holdings, Refinitiv, KLD, Sustainalytics, Morningstar, US EPA, Violation Tracker, ISS, and BoardEx (mostly proprietary).
